summary.title: Evil tip: avoid "easy" things
summary.one_liner: Working on tasks perceived as hard earns credit and help, while "easy" tasks bring little reward, and postponing unavoidable easy work until it becomes urgent can shrink its scope.
keywords: how to look like a hero at work
takeaways: Perceived difficulty, not actual difficulty, determines the reward: hard-looking work earns help, resources and credit.
Easy tasks are a lose-lose situation, since failure is shameful and success goes unremarked.
Postponing an unavoidable easy task until it is urgent makes it look harder and shrinks its scope.
Being gracious when colleagues remind you late discourages them from reminding you earlier next time.
The author frames these as satirical 'evil' tips and notes the risks of being seen as a hero or of resentment.
summary.summary: This is a satirical essay by Yossi Kreinin in which the author argues that people's perception of task difficulty drives career outcomes: working on "hard"-seeming things earns help and credit, while easy ones are thankless. It introduces the "postponing gambit," where unavoidable easy work is delayed until it becomes urgent, which both makes it look harder and reduces its scope, with suggested excuses and ways to keep colleagues from reminding you early. The piece also includes a short anecdote about a manager refusing to believe someone admits to postponing work, and closes with the advice to keep perceived-easy things off your list. The tone is ironic throughout, so the tips are best read as commentary on workplace politics rather than literal guidance.
